newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ retail sector seen running on flat despite data.
newsitem.headline: NZ retail sector seen running on flat despite data.

text.p: New Zealand's retail sector remains in a trough despite encouraging data for April that showed a higher-than-expected rise in sales, analysts said on Tuesday.
Analysts argued that the monthly series was too volatile to support any firm conclusions and a clearer picture came from the trend of the last few months, which was flat.

"We wouldn't be telling people that the time has come, the economy has turned. But it's further evidence that we are troughing along the bottom," said Warren Couillault, retail analyst at brokers SBC Warburg.
Nevertheless, the trend rise in April was at least a good sign for a sector that has endured six months of flat sales.

Statistics New Zealand said earlier in the day that seasonally adjusted retail sales rose 7.9 percent in April, compared with a 3.9 percent fall in March and following a 0.5 percent rise in April 1996.
Market expectations had varied widely from a 2.0 percent fall to a 5.0 percent rise, the average being a 1.38 percent rise.
"You've got to look at the trend over the last two or three months," Bankers Trust NZ chief economist David Plank said, looking at the possible trend information in the data.
Weakness in February and March was over stated, as was April's strength, Plank said.
More importantly, the three months to April had been flat, which was consistent with the results seen in consumer confidence surveys, he added.
BTNZ does not expect any pick-up until the year's end.
SBC Warburg's Couillault said anecdotal evidence suggested there was no definite uptrend in sales.
The last six months had been close to the bottom of the trend and the next six to 12 months were likely to see a clear bottoming out and then a pick-up, he said.
The exception were retailers who experienced "secular" growth outside the constraints of the economy.

In that category, companies like newly listed fast food chain Restaurant Brands, which runs the former Pepsico franchises of Pizza Hut and KFC, were picking up more than their share of retail spending.
"You also get companies that might be taking a lot of costs out at the moment that will have increasing leverage when the market picks up," Couillault said.
"Then you get companies such as (discount retailer) The Warehouse, which just is steaming ahead in spite of no big increase in same-store sales or people flooding into the stores," he said.
"The reason they are still growing well, apart from their capacity expansion, is that they are filling up their stores with new product ranges," he said.

"The potential of The Warehouse is so untapped because you've got a huge franchise. If they can roll more categories through the stores then people will still go there but for a wider range of product," he said.
Official data aside, home appliance retailer Pacific Retail said last week that sales volumes had remained depressed, which put its focus back on improved operating margins.
Supermarket chain Progressive Enterprises, which is in a restructuring phase, said in May that sales were down in its third quarter to April.
Progressive is nevertheless expected to recover strongly in the current year due to ongoing re-positioning, analysts say.
